lines: Every commit you've watched so far touched a whole file — adding one, or swapping one out entirely for a newer version.
But what happens when a change only needs to touch a handful of rows buried inside a file that's otherwise still correct? That's today's real question.
Here's the setup. A tiny slice of a table's rows needs updating, and those rows happen to be scattered across nearly every file the table owns.
What's actually the cheapest way to get that change committed?
answer: There isn't a single right answer here — there are two entirely different, both legitimate, strategies in real use.
Neither one is simply better. Each one just moves the expense to a different place in the pipeline.

lines: Take the first strategy. Any file that holds even a single changed row gets an entirely new version written for it, full stop.
Nothing partial ever gets touched, and nothing like a little patch note gets left behind — no separate log file exists anywhere.
This wasn't just asserted — it was actually run. A change touching about one in every hundred rows was applied for real, scattered across a dozen files.
Every single file holding a changed row got rewritten in full, and the real wall-clock cost of doing that was measured directly.
Now here's a fair question worth sitting with. All that expensive rewriting at write time — does it actually earn something back later, when someone reads the table?
Or is reading just as costly either way, no matter how recently those files were rewritten?
answer: It absolutely earns something back. Because every file is already guaranteed current, a read never has anything extra to reconcile.
There's no second source to double check, no patch to apply on the way past — a read just opens the files and trusts them completely.

lines: Here's the opposite philosophy entirely. Instead of rewriting anything, the change gets written to its own small separate file, off to the side.
That original file stays frozen, untouched, exactly as it already was — the new information only gets reconciled with it later, whenever someone actually reads.
The exact same one-in-a-hundred change, run for real under this opposite approach, told a very different story.
Writing it cost almost nothing by comparison. But reading afterward got measurably, repeatedly more expensive with every additional round of changes left sitting unreconciled.
So what clears that growing debt away? A deliberate housekeeping pass that finally folds every one of those little side files back into the originals, for good.
Run for real here too — after five rounds of deferred changes got folded in at once, that reading cost collapsed right back down to almost nothing.
Here's what's worth noticing: every major table format independently arrived at this identical fork in the road, just dressed up in its own vocabulary.
One vendor calls its side-file approach a deletion vector. Another just names the two whole strategies outright. Underneath the naming, it's the same exact trade, every time.
So the whole decision boils down to one simple question: pay the cost now, while writing, or hand that bill to whoever reads next?
How often rows change, how scattered those changes are across your files, and how fresh a reader actually needs their data to be — that's genuinely the entire decision.
